st.headline: Tech rebounds; Seatrium retrenches over 200 staff; StarHub, M1 to merge: Markets this week
st.teaser: Investors are still watching the tech space, as well as proposed US tariffs on Singapore and 13 other trading partners.
fullText: SINGAPORE – Global markets and Singapore stocks rebounded when the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia chief executive was announced on Nov 24, after days of sell-offs in tech and artificial intelligence stocks that wiped the entire year’s gains from the NASDAQ.
However, investors are still watching the tech space, as well as proposed US tariffs on Singapore and 13 other trading partners.
Tech stocks rallied after news of Huang’s return, with Singapore-listed counters like Mi Material and PC Partner seeing shares stage double-digit jumps over the trading session of Nov 24.

The gains eased by the end of the week, with Mi Material up 5.8% and PC Partner up 2% at the Nov 27 close. Other tech stocks also ended higher, with AEM up 3.6% to $6.09 and semiconductor manufacturer UMS 2.5% higher at $1.64.

After an initial rally, US markets continued to be volatile ahead of the Thanksgiving weekend following news of new US tariffs. The S&P 500 was down around 2.8% over the week, while NASDAQ was down nearly 5%.

The Huang saga exposed the fault lines in corporate governance, board independence and succession planning, and fanned concerns about big tech and the massive amount of funds poured into AI investments.

His swift return – when the dust had barely settled after his Nov 12 resignation following reports about his affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy – was reportedly slammed by critics and lawmakers in the US, who questioned the independence of the board.
On Nov 25, S&P Global Ratings placed Nvidia’s credit rating on watch for a possible downgrade, bringing up questions of management and board oversight.

The Financial Times reported on Nov 26, citing insiders, that Nvidia has told manufacturing partners to stop shipping servers containing its chips to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia after new US export controls on advanced AI chips to some South-east Asian countries.
Singapore has not confirmed if Nvidia shipments to the Republic have indeed been stopped, Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said the next day.

He added that the Government is engaging local companies to assess the impact of the US’ latest chip curbs, and is working with the US to explore how companies here can continue having secured access to high-end chips.
Meanwhile, Singapore has objected to the findings of a probe behind the US’ proposal to impose tariffs of up to 20% on the Republic and 13 other trading partners under Section 301.
The US Trade Representative accused the countries of producing more goods than they would under normal, market-oriented conditions.
The Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry said on Nov 26 that the findings fail to account for Singapore’s open, trade-reliant economic structure.

The duties could take effect in early 2027, though the US Trade Representative’s Jamieson Greer offered to consider lowering the proposed rate to 10% if Singapore reaches an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade with Washington.

The Singapore Business Federation expressed concerns not only about the absolute tariff rate but also about how potential differences in rates between Singapore and competing economies could affect businesses’ competitiveness and future investment and supply-chain decisions.

“We recognise that there remains room for further negotiations and hope that continued engagement will lead to an outcome that takes into account Singapore’s circumstances as a small and highly open economy,” it said on Nov 26.
On the home front, Seatrium will lay off around 2% of its Singapore workforce, or about 220 staff, as it streamlines global operations and consolidates its network of yards.

Seatrium, which is a Singapore-listed offshore, marine and energy group, said it is transforming systems and processes in line with future business needs, which includes speeding up the optimisation of facilities in Singapore, where it has five yards.
Globally, Seatrium has pared its yards from 15 in 2023 to the current 11.

In Singapore, it will wind down operations of its Admiralty yard by 2028, and refocus its Benoi, Pioneer and Tuas yards on work that supports the group’s global projects, such as higher-value repairs and upgrades. Its flagship yard remains the one at Tuas Boulevard.

This is Seatrium’s first workforce restructuring exercise since it was formed in 2023 through the merger of Sembcorp Marine and Keppel Offshore & Marine. Its global headcount in August 2025 stood at about 24,000.
Its shares fell over 7% immediately after the announcement of the layoffs, but pared the losses to 1.5% on Nov 27.
Still, analysts remained optimistic on the stock, with OCBC equity research analyst Rachel Miu maintaining a “buy” call.

She noted that the recent sell-off is driven by order book concern and compounded by a workforce and yard restructuring announcement that the market interpreted as a demand signal rather than operational efficiency.
“However, the company won an FPSO integration contract from Modec for Guyana in November, a positive signal for pipeline activity, though the contract value was not disclosed,” she said.
She also noted that this announcement came after two new projects were announced in October, with a total value of $700 million.

“During the recent business update, the management indicated that new order flow depends largely on the project owners’ timetable. The management also indicated that cost savings, or cost discipline, is an ongoing process to support a leaner and more efficient structure,” she said.
Seatrium is also actively exploring new projects, such as with Bermuda-based company Golar LNG, she noted.

StarHub will merge with M1 in a deal worth $1.1 billion, the telco said on Nov 24. The merger is slated to be completed in the first half of 2027, subject to regulatory approval by the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA).

cna.headline: Seoul monitoring signs of possible Kim Jong Un visit to China
cna.teaser: Seoul monitoring signs of possible Kim Jong Un visit to China
fullText: SEOUL: South Korea's spy agency said on Saturday (Nov 28) it was monitoring "various developments" about a possible visit to China by North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, following reports on such a trip. China is North Korea's largest trading partner and a vital source of diplomatic, economic and political support for Pyongyang, although ties have not always been smooth. Kim made an unannounced, one-day visit to the Chinese border city of Dandong in October, crossing a major bridge linking China and nuclear-armed North Korea that is widely considered a symbol of their deepening economic ties. A South Korean broadcaster KBS, citing an unnamed diplomatic source, reported that Chinese President Xi Jinping told his South Korean counterpart Lee Jae Myung during their summit earlier this month that Kim could visit China. Citing an unnamed government source, it also reported that an "emergency order" had been issued in the Chinese border city of Dandong, echoing arrangements made for Kim's October visit.

Seoul's spy agency told AFP Saturday it was "keeping a close eye on various developments", when asked about the report. Seoul's presidential office said Xi did not mention what was described by the KBS report, adding that the administration "is closely monitoring developments in North Korea-China relations". Despite long-running UN sanctions, North Korea has enshrined its status as a nuclear-armed state in law, with its regime repeatedly declaring its atomic arsenal permanent and irreversible. Kim has ignored repeated overtures for talks from US President Donald Trump, who has said a meeting was "up to" China's Xi. Experts say Pyongyang is effectively demanding US recognition as a nuclear-armed state as a precondition for talks -- a concession they say would pose complex diplomatic and security challenges for Washington, a key ally of Seoul. A visit to China could give Kim an opportunity to discuss with Xi the outcome of the recent US-China talks and trilateral summit involving Russia, another key ally of Pyongyang, experts say.
Our chief editor shares analysis and picks of the week's biggest news every Saturday.

economistArticle.title: The fall of China’s most trusted wealth manager
paras: For over a decade, CreditEase stood as a titan of China's burgeoning wealth management industry, promising affluent individuals steady returns in a turbulent domestic market. Founded in the heyday of financial innovation, the firm expanded aggressively by channeling private capital into real estate ventures and high-yielding shadow banking instruments. Yet, what was once celebrated as a paragon of private financial acumen has abruptly unraveled under the weight of mounting asset defaults and intense regulatory scrutiny.

The firm's rapid downfall underscores systemic vulnerabilities embedded deep within China's non-bank financial architecture. As property developers defaulted on debt obligations and real estate valuations plummeted, the high-yield trusts that underpinned CreditEase's investment portfolios turned toxic. Wealthy clients who had trusted the firm's prestigious brand and glowing historic track record were left stranded when redemption payments were suspended without advance warning.

Beijing's regulatory authorities have decisively curtailed the operational latitude previously enjoyed by non-state asset managers. Regulators are prioritizing financial system stability over emergency bailouts, signaling to high-net-worth investors that private institutions are no longer protected by implicit state guarantees. The collapse of CreditEase serves as a sobering reminder that shadow banking promises of risk-free yields belong to a bygone economic era.

For China's middle and upper classes, the fallout is both financially painful and psychologically jarring. Deprived of trusted wealth-preservation vehicles, affluent households are increasingly shifting capital into low-yield cash deposits or overseas assets. Private wealth management firms across the region must now operate within a redefined landscape marked by strict regulatory compliance, diminished investor sentiment, and vastly subdued return expectations.

Ultimately, the demise of CreditEase marks a decisive turning point in China's financial trajectory. As the era of double-digit investment yields closes, private investors are being forced to embrace genuine risk assessment in a moderating economy. The fall of this former financial giant demonstrates that public trust, once eroded in the capital markets, is extraordinarily difficult to rebuild.
economistArticle.cn:
十多年来，宜信（CreditEase）一直是中国蓬勃发展的财富管理行业的巨头，在动荡的国内市场中向富裕阶层承诺稳定的回报。该公司成立于金融创新的鼎盛时期，通过将私人资本引入房地产项目和高收益的影子银行产品迅速扩张。然而，这一曾被誉为民营金融智慧典范的企业，在资产违约加剧和监管审查企稳的重压下，骤然崩溃。

该公司的迅速衰落凸显了中国非银行金融体系深层固有的系统性脆弱性。随着房地产开发商出现债务违约、房地产估值大幅下跌，支撑宜信投资组合的高收益信托变成了不良资产。信任该公司显赫品牌和过去辉煌业绩的富裕客户，在赎回计划未经预警即被暂停时陷入了困境。

北京的监管机构已果断缩减了民营资产管理公司此前享有的操作自由度。监管部门正优先考虑金融体系的稳定性而非紧急救助，向高净值投资者明确信号：民营机构不再享有隐性国家担保。宜信的倒闭是一个令人警醒的信号，表明影子银行无风险高收益的承诺已成为过去时代的遗迹。

对于中国的中产和富裕阶层而言，这一后果既带来了经济上的痛楚，也造成了心理上的冲击。由于缺乏值得信赖的保值渠道，富裕家庭正日益将资金转向低收益的现金存款或海外资产。该地区的民营财富管理公司如今必须在一个以严格合规、投资者情绪低迷和预期回报率大幅放缓为特征的新环境中生存。

归根结底，宜信的败落标志着中国金融发展轨迹上的一个决定性转折点。随着两位数投资回报时代的终结，在经济增速放缓的环境下，私人投资者被迫直面真正的风险评估。这家昔日金融巨头的陨落表明，资本市场中的公共信任一旦破灭，极难重构。
